title: Context engineering: what goes on the desk
hook: Paste, retrieve, summarize, call tools, structure, and cache. Deciding what the model sees.
inPlainWords: Everything the model knows about your task on a given call is what you put in its context. Context engineering is choosing what goes in, in what order, and what to leave out. It is often the biggest lever on quality, cost and speed.

useCase.title: Answer a hard, escalated case
useCase.story: An escalated case has a 200-message history, the customer's profile, three policy documents, product manuals and live order data. The model can only take part of it, and answers get worse when the desk is cluttered.

approaches.name: Paste everything
approaches.avoidWhen: Large cases. It is slow, costly and distracting.

approaches.name: Retrieve only what is relevant
approaches.what: Search for the parts this question needs (RAG).
approaches.example: Pull the two relevant policy paragraphs.

approaches.name: Summarize older material
approaches.what: Compress history and keep recent detail.
approaches.avoidWhen: Details matter, and summaries lose them.
approaches.example: A summary of messages 1 to 180, plus the last 20 in full.

approaches.name: Use tools for live facts
approaches.what: Ask the systems, not the model's memory.
approaches.avoidWhen: Static text. Use retrieval for that.

approaches.name: Structure and order the context
approaches.what: Use clear sections, with key instructions and the question placed prominently.
approaches.example: Headings: Customer, History summary, Policy, Live data, Question.

approaches.name: Cache the stable parts
approaches.what: Reuse the unchanging beginning of the prompt.
approaches.example: Reuse the system instructions across calls.

approaches.name: Separate instructions from data
approaches.what: Mark outside text as data, not commands.
approaches.example: Wrap the customer's email in a data section.

challenge.question: How should you assemble the context for the escalated case?

options.text: A structured prompt: instructions, a summary of old history plus recent messages in full, retrieved policy passages, live data from tools, and untrusted text marked as data
options.why: Each piece is chosen, ordered and labeled for the job.
It might work, but it is slow, costly and noisy.
It loses the history that explains the case.

options.text: Rely on the model remembering earlier chats

bestCase.title: Choose, order and label what the model sees
bestCase.example: The prompt has clear sections: instructions, a summary of messages 1 to 180, the last 20 in full, two retrieved policy paragraphs, live order data, and the customer's message marked as data. Answers are sharper, and the bill is lower.

worstCase.title: A cluttered desk
worstCase.example: All 200 messages and three full manuals are pasted in. The model answers an old question from the middle of the thread, ignores the newest message, and the call takes ten times longer.

steps.label: Gather the sources
steps.goes: History, profile, policies, manuals, live data.

steps.label: Choose what fits
steps.goes: Summarize old messages, retrieve two policy passages, fetch live order data.
steps.goesWrong: Everything is pasted in, filling the window with noise.

steps.label: Order and label sections
steps.goes: Clear headings, with the question prominent.

steps.label: Mark customer text as data
steps.goes: Outside text cannot act as commands.

steps.label: Model answers
steps.goes: It works from a tidy, relevant desk.

steps.label: Log what it saw
steps.goes: The exact context is saved for debugging.

takeaway: The quality of an answer depends on what is on the desk. Choose it, order it, label it, and log it.
